Science · 21 November 2026

When psychology put itself to the test

In 2015, hundreds of researchers repeated a hundred published studies. The result shook the discipline and has made it more rigorous.

One of the basic rules of science is that a result must be repeatable. If an experiment only works once, it may have been chance. A decade ago, psychology decided to check how far its findings met that rule.

A hundred studies, a surprise

In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration, a group of around 270 researchers coordinated by Brian Nosek, repeated 100 studies published in leading psychology journals. They followed the original methods and, where possible, consulted the authors. Only about 36% of the replications produced a statistically significant result in the same direction, and the effects were on average half as large.

Why it happened

In most cases it was not fraud. The problems were more ordinary: small samples, the temptation to try many analyses until one was "significant", and journals' tendency to publish striking results rather than those that found nothing. The problem is not unique to psychology: it has also been seen in medicine, economics and biology.

What has changed

  • Pre-registration: before collecting data, researchers publish what they will measure and how they will analyse it.
  • Larger samples and projects run across many laboratories at once.
  • Open data, so others can check the analyses.
  • Registered reports: the journal accepts the study before the result is known.

Some famous effects, such as power posing or certain kinds of priming, have not held up. Others, such as the Stroop effect, anchoring or spaced practice, have been confirmed again and again. At Psycholopedia we try to say which findings are solid and which are in doubt. A science that reviews its own results is not showing weakness; it is showing that it works.

References

  1. Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science, 349(6251), aac4716.
  2. Nosek, B. A. et al. (2018). The preregistration revolution. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(11), 2600–2606.
